intro: You need to optimize photos for faster website loading to keep your visitors and search engines happy. If your full resolution files are dragging down your portfolio speed, you are losing potential clients.

blocks.text: The cost of a broken image compression workflow

Your time is your most valuable asset. When you manually handle every file for every platform, you create a bottleneck. You spend hours sitting at your desk, dragging sliders and waiting for progress bars. This is not creative work. This is data management that drains your energy.

The financial cost is hidden but real. If you spend 15 hours a week on these tasks, you lose 780 hours a year. That is almost 20 full work weeks. You could use that time to shoot more, meet clients, or simply rest. The physical cost is also high. Prolonged desk time leads to neck pain, eye strain, and repetitive strain injuries. You are trading your health for manual labor that a computer should do for you.
Why image optimization feels like a struggle

The main issue is a confusion between archival and delivery. You treat every export like a master file. You save everything at maximum quality. Then, you try to shrink those huge files for the web. This leads to poor results. You get files that are either too large to load or so compressed that they look muddy.

Another cause is platform fragmentation. Instagram, Facebook, and your own website all have different requirements. If you upload a file that is too large, the platform re-compresses it. This causes artifact stacking. The image loses detail and color depth. You end up with a blurry, pixelated version of your hard work.
Fixes anyone can use for free

items: Standardize your export presets. Create a specific preset for web that caps the long edge at 2000 pixels.
Use the built-in Preview app on your Mac. Open a folder of images, select all with ⌘ A, then go to File > Export Selected Images to change formats quickly.
Download ImageOptim. It is free and open source. Drag and drop your folder of JPEGs onto it to strip out metadata and reduce file size without losing visible quality.
Resize before you compress. If your website container is 1080 pixels wide, do not upload a 4000 pixel file. Shrink it in Photoshop or Lightroom first.
Check your color profiles. Convert everything to sRGB before saving for the web to ensure colors look consistent across all browsers.

faq.question: Does image compression ruin my photos?
faq.answer: It only ruins them if you overwrite your original files. Always keep your full resolution RAW files in a separate folder. Only compress copies intended for web or client delivery.

faq.question: What is the best file format for web?
faq.answer: JPEG is still the most compatible. WebP offers better compression but may not work in every single legacy application. Use JPEG for general portfolios and WebP if you need maximum speed.
